extracted.intended_audience: students, journalists, political scientists, and general readers interested in public opinion and political communication
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how public opinion is formed and how mental pictures (pseudo-environments), symbols, news, and education shape political behavior and decision-making. The rubric covers how reporters, teachers, politicians, and institutions should supply, check, and correct the pictures on which people act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition of the pseudo-environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that people act on a 'pseudo-environment' — representations or pictures of the world made by humans — rather than on direct knowledge of the real environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann: 'It is the insertion between man and his environment of a pseudo-environment. To that pseudo-environment his behavior is a response.' Analysts must account for how constructed pictures (from hallucination to schematic scientific models) drive thought, feeling, and action; maladjustment occurs when actions based on pseudo-environments meet the real environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triangular framework: scene, picture, response
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin analysis by recognizing the triangular relationship between the scene of action (the real environment), the human picture of that scene (the pseudo‑environment), and the human response to that picture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analyst must treat public behaviour as a drama where interior motive (mental picture) and external behavior interact; understanding all three parts is essential to explain and predict action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish fiction from lies and account for fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between 'fictions' (representations of the environment with varying degrees of fidelity) and deliberate lies; a fiction can be useful if its degree of fidelity is understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictions run from hallucination to schematic scientific models; the 'degree of fidelity' should be taken into account so that fiction is not misleading. The alternative to using fictions (direct sensation) is impractical given complexity of the environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and dynamics of symbols and stereotyping
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that symbolic pictures (heroes, devils, allegories) organize emotion and behavior and that symbols coalesce, fracture, and compete in the public mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Symbols can have enormous practical force (e.g., hero-worship of leaders); in normal times symbols are less inclusive and subject to check, comparison, and argument. Analysts should trace how symbols are constructed and how they govern behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Importance of authoritative, valid intelligence/reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Public opinion and effective criticism depend on 'intelligence work' — expert reporters and valid pictures of the environment supplied to critics, teachers, and decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without reliable intelligence the critic's dialectic is limited. Lippmann calls for organized collection of social knowledge so political science and civic education can use it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher’s/civic education responsibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: Civic education should prepare pupils to understand how their minds construct pictures and to examine the sources and character of their information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the case method; teach students to inspect where dispatches were filed, the correspondent's name, the press service, authority for statements, and the circumstances of acquisition; teach the character of censorship and propaganda and the habit of introspection about imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine news-source metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: When evaluating a news report, check metadata: where the dispatch was filed, the correspondent's identity, the press service, authority cited, and circumstances under which the statement was secured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teachers should inculcate habits of looking for these items; they are practical tools to judge the reliability of a report and to detect deliberate deception or sloppiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask whether the reporter witnessed events
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether the reporter actually saw what is described and remember how that reporter has characterized past events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a concrete check against accepting fiction as fact and helps to evaluate eyewitness reliability and the limits of secondhand dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach awareness of censorship, privacy, and propaganda
rubrics_metrics.description: Educate about the effects and signs of censorship, privacy constraints, and past propaganda so citizens can better interpret present reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of past propaganda and censorship practices inoculates against naive acceptance of stereotyped pictures; teachers should include comparative history and anthropology to show how codes shape imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect allegorizing, dramatizing, and personification
rubrics_metrics.description: Train people to catch themselves making allegories, dramatizing relations, and personifying abstractions when forming opinions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifying these rhetorical/compositional moves helps reveal how imagery shapes emotional response and may misrepresent complex realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic gathering of social knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocate systematic, non-haphazard collection of social data as a normal accompaniment to action so political science can generalize and education can prepare citizens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann urges that information collection will be done because decisions require it; accumulated data should be turned into generalizations for schools and civic education.

rubrics_metrics.name: Re-education to align opinion with environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Promote re-education and improved intelligence work to reduce censoring, stereotyping, and dramatizing apparatus and bring public opinion into better contact with reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the relevant environment is knowable, critics and teachers can 'unravel the mind'; where the environment is obscure, intelligence work is required and education alone is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for time-differential between knowledge and action
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize the time differential between discovery/analysis and the need for action; relevance of plans depends on the time required for operation and whether assumed data remain valid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political criticism often becomes hindsight; practical proposals must consider whether the data they rely on will hold over the plan's timespan. The evolution of reason in politics is slower than action demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of appeal to reason in emergencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that in crises the appeal to reason is often ineffective because education and reason evolve slowly; urgent action favors slogans, force, or expedients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'pilot' knowing the right technical course cannot in an emergency make the crew into experts; practical tactics in emergencies (make a speech, use force, offer compromise) may be necessary though not ideal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prejudice and hostile practices are antithetical to reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Condemn hatred, intolerance, suspicion, bigotry, secrecy, fear, and lying as poisons to public reason and appeal to a longer-run view that resists them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While one cannot prove good will will always work, we should hold a 'hearty prejudice' against these vices because they undermine the appeal to reason in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for wide variation in individuals' mental pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: Before explaining behavioral differences between peoples, fix attention on the extraordinary differences in what men know of the world — i.e., their different pseudo-environments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caution against generalizing about 'what man is' until there is measurable similarity in environments; pseudo-environments are hybrids of 'human nature' and conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propaganda as picture-substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Define propaganda as the deliberate effort to alter the picture to which men respond — i.e., to substitute one social pattern for another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize how organized propaganda aims to form class- or national-consciousness; evaluation should examine the techniques and fidelity of propagated pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize manufactured public personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect that public personalities (heroes, regal selves) are often constructed and that public perception of leaders may be more myth than reality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Biographies and public images frequently present separate selves (public/regal vs private/human). Communicators and analysts should be aware of stage-managed facades and their political effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check partisan need as a motive for accepting fictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be alert to the fact that people and institutions often accept and act on fictions because those pictures are 'much needed' by their partisan aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lippmann's example of Senators accepting a rumor because it supported partisan aims illustrates how emotional need accelerates credulity; analysts must separate evidentiary form from desire for the fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use historical study of error as preventive and pedagogic tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach the study of error — past superstitions, misinterpretations, and stereotypes — as a prophylactic that encourages appreciation of objective scientific method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting scientific method as victories over superstition can inspire curiosity and reduce attachment to prejudices; destruction of prejudice enlarges attention and supports civic understanding.
